title: Data and the vocabulary
html:
Purpose. Nearly every formula in this book uses the same few symbols. Learn them once here. Also learn why data quality and honest testing matter more than any algorithm.

Key ideas

  • A dataset is a table. A row is one example, a column is one feature, and one special column is the target (the label).
  • Parameters are learned by training. Hyperparameters are chosen by you before training.
  • Always test on data the model never saw. Split the data into training, validation and test sets.
  • Before building a model, measure a trivial baseline. A model that does not beat it is useless.

3.1 A dataset is a table

Here are five rows of a loan-offers table. The values are made up for illustration.

# OfferedAmount (EUR) NumberOfTerms CreditScore Accepted (target)
1 10,000 36 720 1
2 25,000 60 650 0
3 5,000 24 780 1
4 40,000 84 600 0
5 15,000 48 690 1

Columns 1 to 3 are the inputs (features). The last column is what you want to predict (the target, or label). Each row is one training example. A model learns from the rows where the target is known, and is then used on new rows where it is not.

3.2 Notation

Symbol Meaning In the table above
m number of training examples 5
n number of features 3
x the input features the first three columns
y the target, the true answer the Accepted column
(x^(i), y^(i)) the i-th training example (the superscript is a row number, not a power) row 2: x^(2) = [25000, 60, 650], y^(2) = 0
x^(i)_j feature j of example i x^(2)_3 = 650
f(x) or y-hat the model's prediction what the model says for a row
w, b the parameters (weights and bias) learned by training

A vector is just a list of numbers. x^(2) is the vector of all features of the second row.

3.3 Parameters and hyperparameters

Parameters are the numbers the algorithm learns: w and b in a line, the weights in a neural network. Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training and that training does not change: the learning rate, the number of passes over the data (epochs), K in nearest neighbours, the regularization strength, the polynomial degree. You find good hyperparameters by trying values and measuring on held-out data, not by guessing (Shaw Talebi).

3.4 Train, validation and test sets

A model that scores well on the examples it was fitted to has proved nothing, just as a student who sees the exam questions in advance proves nothing. You need data the model has never seen:

Set Used for Typical share
Training fitting the parameters 60 to 80%
Validation choosing hyperparameters and comparing models 10 to 20%
Test one final honest score, used once at the end 10 to 20%

Two rules that save careers. First, fit any preparation step (such as scaling) on the training set only, then apply it to the others. Fitting it on everything lets information from the test rows leak into training. Second, for data that has a time order, such as loans, split by date: train on the past, test on the future. A random split lets the model peek at the future and flatters it. Chapter 12 goes deeper.

3.5 Data quality

Machine learning is only as good as its data: garbage in, garbage out. Good data has quantity (too few examples lead to overfitting, Chapter 11) and quality (Shaw Talebi):

  • Accurate. An age of 35 that should be 53, or an income of $12,000 that is really per month, teaches the model something false.
  • Diverse and representative. A churn model trained only on Pro users will fail on Enterprise customers.

Beyond the videos. Three traps that are especially common in lending:

  • Selection bias. You only know whether people repaid if you approved them. A model trained on approved loans has never seen the rejected ones.
  • Leakage. A feature that is only known after the outcome, such as a collections status, makes a model look brilliant in testing and useless in production. Always ask: would I have this value at the moment of the decision?
  • Label noise. The target itself can be wrong or defined inconsistently, for example "default" meaning 60 days late in one system and 90 in another.

3.6 Always measure a baseline

A baseline is the simplest sensible prediction: for regression, predict the average of the training targets; for classification, predict the most common class. If 95% of offers are accepted, a model that always says "accepted" is 95% accurate and completely useless. Your model has to beat the baseline by a margin that matters, or it is not earning its complexity.

Loan example. In the table above, three of five offers are accepted (60%). A baseline that always predicts "accepted" is right 60% of the time. Any classifier you build on this table must beat 60%, measured on rows it did not train on.

Common mistakes

  • Scoring a model on its training data, and then being surprised in production.
  • Scaling or cleaning the whole dataset before splitting it (leakage).
  • Random-splitting time-ordered data.
  • Skipping the baseline.

Check yourself

  • In the offers table, what are m and n, and what is x^(3)?
  • What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter? Give an example of each.
  • Why must a test set be used only once, at the end?
  • Give an example of leakage in a loan model.
Show answers

(1) m = 5, n = 3, x^(3) = [5000, 24, 780]. (2) A parameter is learned (a weight w); a hyperparameter is chosen by you (the learning rate). (3) If you tune on it, it stops being unseen data and the score becomes too optimistic. (4) Using "days in collections" to predict default: you only know it after the default has started.

Go deeper: Google's Rules of Machine Learning (practical, written by engineers) · the scikit-learn pages on cross-validation and preprocessing · An Introduction to Statistical Learning, free book.
